title: Clocha na nAinmneacha
subtitle: The Stones of Names — Maigh Eo, c. 480 AD

sessions.en: The first greeting, and who you are

paras: Salt wind. A field above the grey Atlantic, County Mayo, around the year 480. A man kneels at a long pillar of stone, cutting notches into its edge with a chisel of iron. Wood smoke, wet grass, the tap-tap-tap of careful work.
He looks up, unhurried, and raises a hand.
“[Dia dhuit!](turas://g/0)”

blocks.title: The greeting is younger than the stone
paras: That greeting is *new* here. Christianity reached this coast within living memory, and it rewired how people say hello: **Dia dhuit** — “God to you.”
The custom is call-and-response, and the response *raises* the greeting:
You never just echo a greeting in Irish. You answer it, and add to it.
pairs: — Dia is Muire dhuit.  (God *and Mary* to you.)

blocks.prompt: The carver said “Dia dhuit.” What do you say back?

opts.why: You raised the greeting — God and Mary to you. Exactly the custom.
Understandable — but Irish greetings escalate. The reply adds Mary: Dia is Muire dhuit.
That's “goodbye” — a little early, you only just met him.

paras: He sets down the chisel and puts a hand to his chest.
“[Is mise Dáire.](turas://g/0)” A pause. A nod at you. “[Cé thusa?](turas://g/1)”

glosses.g: I am Dáire — ‘is mise’ introduces who you are

blocks.title: The two “to be”s — what school never explained
paras: Irish has **two** verbs where English has one “to be”, and they are not interchangeable.
**Is** — the copula — is for *identity*: who or what something *is*.
**Tá** is for *states and conditions*: how something is right now.
You are not “in a state of being Niamh” — you simply *are* Niamh. Identity takes **is**. Half the confusion of school Irish dissolves right here.
pairs: Is mise Dáire. — I am Dáire.
Tá mé fuar. — I am cold.

blocks.prompt: How would Bríd say “I am Bríd”?

opts.why: Identity → the copula. Is mise Bríd.
Tá is for states — cold, tired, happy. Being Bríd isn't a passing condition; identity takes is.
Irish word order is strict here: Is mise Bríd.

blocks.prompt: Build: “I am Áine.”
Your turn. Answer the carver — introduce yourself.
blocks.hint: Type the whole phrase: Is mise + your name.

paras: He repeats your name once, slowly, weighing it the way other people weigh coins — then glances at the pillar beside him, its edge already striped with strokes.
“Names are my trade,” he says. “I cut them so they outlive the breath that spoke them.”

“[Cén t-ainm atá ort?](turas://g/0)” he adds — and notice the shape of that: in Irish, a name is *on* you, like a cloak. The language keeps a small distance between you and what you're called. More on that another day.

glosses.g: What's your name? — literally ‘what name is on you?’

blocks.prompt: Match the Irish to its meaning.

paras: The light is going. Dáire covers his tools with a hide and lifts a hand.
“[Slán go fóill.](turas://g/0)” — goodbye *for now*. Tomorrow he'll want to know where you come from. Have an answer ready.

sessions.en: Where you're from — placenames are poems

paras: Morning. The tide far out, oystercatchers crying over the flats. Dáire is already at the stone.
“[Cé as thú?](turas://g/0)”
He answers his own question first, the way a courteous man does: “[Is as Maigh Eo mé.](turas://g/1)”

glosses.g: Where are you from? — lit. ‘who from are you?’ (Connacht; you'll also see Cárb as thú?)
I am from Mayo — Maigh Eo, ‘plain of the yew trees’

blocks.title: Every placename is a tiny poem
paras: **Maigh Eo** — the plain of the yews. Dáire's county is named for trees that stood before anyone carved anything.
Nearly every Irish placename works like this — a small, worn poem hiding inside the English spelling:
And if your people left, the poems travelled: Dublin, Ohio. Derry, New Hampshire. You may have grown up inside an Irish placename without knowing it.
pairs: Baile Átha Cliath — town of the hurdle ford  (Dublin)
Béal Feirste — mouth of the sandbank ford  (Belfast)
Cill Dara — church of the oak  (Kildare)

blocks.prompt: You want to ask someone where they're from. Which is it?

opts.why: Literally “who from are you?” — the Connacht way to ask.
Close — but that asks who they are, not where they're from.
That's hello. A fine start, but it won't get you a county.

blocks.prompt: Match the place to the poem inside it.
Build: “I am from Galway.”
Now answer Dáire — where are you from? Anywhere in the world counts.
blocks.hint: Is as ___ mé — put your county, city or country in the middle.

paras: He nods at your answer as if adding it to a ledger, and spreads both hands wide:
“[Céad míle fáilte.](turas://g/0)”
A hundred thousand welcomes. People will still be saying it on this island fifteen centuries from now — to tourists, mostly, but they'll mean it.

blocks.prompt: Quick return to yesterday — and one new word.

paras: As you leave, Dáire mentions that a family is walking in from the east tomorrow, bringing him work: a stone for a man who died in the spring.
“Come early,” he says. “You'll see what the stones are *for*.”

sessions.en: Son and daughter — your surname was carved first

paras: They arrive mid-morning: a widow in a dark cloak, her grown son beside her, walking like a man carrying something heavier than the satchel on his back. They have come to order a stone.
A girl of about twelve slips out from behind the workshop wall and stands at Dáire's elbow, openly studying you.

“[Seo Bríd, m'iníon.](turas://g/0)” He nods at the visiting young man. “And that is Colmán's [mac](turas://g/1) — his son. No [deartháir](turas://g/2), no [deirfiúr](turas://g/3) — the last of that house.”

glosses.g: This is Bríd, my daughter — iníon = daughter

blocks.title: MAQI — your surname is an ogham formula
paras: On the oldest stones in Ireland, one word appears more than any other: **MAQI** — “of the son”. *X MAQI Y*: X, son of Y. That word is still alive — it became modern Irish **mac**, son.
Which means millions of people are carrying an ogham inscription around on their name:
Women's surnames answer differently: **Ní** (daughter of an Ó family), **Nic** (of a Mac family). Mary Kelly, in Irish, is **Máire Ní Cheallaigh**.
pairs: McCarthy — Mac Cárthaigh — son of Cárthach
O'Brien — Ó Briain — descendant of Brian
Kelly — Ó Ceallaigh — descendant of Ceallach

blocks.prompt: The ogham word MAQI survives today as…

opts.why: Fifteen centuries from stone to surname. Mc and Mac names all carry it.
Ainm is “name” — but MAQI is the word for son, the one carved between names.
Fáilte is welcome. MAQI is the “son of” between two names on a stone.

blocks.prompt: The family, matched.
How would “Mary Kelly” be written in Irish?

opts.why: Ní for a woman of an Ó family — daughter of the Kellys.
Mac marks a son. A woman takes Ní (for Ó names) or Nic (for Mac names).
Ó traditionally marks a male descendant — Mary takes Ní Cheallaigh.

paras: The widow speaks quietly with Dáire, and it is settled. The stone will say who the dead man was in the only way that matters here — by whose son he was:
“[Colmán mac Rónáin.](turas://g/0)”

glosses.g: Colmán, son of Rónán — Rónáin is the ‘of Rónán’ form

blocks.title: Why Rónán became Rónáin
paras: Look closely: Rónán → mac **Rónáin**. Irish names bend their endings to mean *of* — the genitive case. You don't need to master it today; you only need to *recognise* it: when a name shifts shape, it usually means “of”.

blocks.prompt: Set the inscription: “Colmán, son of Rónán.”

paras: The family leaves. Bríd runs her thumb along the blank edge of the pillar where the strokes will go, and looks up at her father, then at you.
“Tomorrow he'll make you *listen*,” she says, delighted. “He always makes them listen first.”

sessions.en: Learning to hear — the secret of Irish spelling

paras: He will not let you near the chisel. Instead he smooths a patch of dust with his palm and scratches letters into it with a stick.
“Before your hand cuts,” he says, “your ear must know what the marks are *for*. Stone doesn't forgive spelling.”

blocks.title: The big secret: every consonant comes in two flavours
paras: Here is the thing that makes Irish look “unpronounceable” — and the moment it stops:
Every Irish consonant has **two sounds** — a **broad** one (leathan) and a **slender** one (caol). The vowels written around it are *signposts* telling you which:
Those “extra” vowels in Irish words aren't decoration and aren't all pronounced — they're **instructions**. Irish spelling isn't chaotic; it's a machine, and you now hold the manual.

blocks.prompt: Which vowels are the broad signposts?

opts.why: Broad: a, o, u. Slender: e, i. That's the whole sorting rule.
Those are the slender pair. Broad is a, o, u.
Fadas mark length, not breadth — the broad set is a, o, u.

blocks.prompt: In the name “Seán”, is the s broad or slender?

opts.txt: Slender — the e beside it says so; it sounds like “sh”
opts.why: Slender s = “sh”. That's why Seán is “Shawn” — the e was the instruction.

opts.txt: Broad — it's just an s sound
opts.why: The e beside it is a slender signpost: slender s sounds like “sh”. Seán = “Shawn”.

blocks.title: An síneadh fada — the long mark
paras: The accent — **á é í ó ú** — is called the **síneadh fada**, “the long stretch”. It lengthens the vowel, and it is never optional, because it changes meaning:
Drop a fada and you may turn a man into grass, or an old thing into a person. The dead of Chapter 1 would want their names spelled right; so do the living.

blocks.prompt: “Tá féar ann” — there is ___ there.

opts.why: féar = grass. fear (no fada) would be a man. The mark does real work.
That would be fear, no fada. féar — long é — is grass.

blocks.prompt: In “cáil” (fame), is the c broad or slender?

opts.txt: Broad — á is a broad signpost
opts.why: a/o/u (with or without fada) mean broad. Broad c, like English “caw”.

opts.txt: Slender — the i makes it slender
opts.why: The signpost that matters is the one beside the consonant: c sits next to á. Broad.

blocks.prompt: Dáire scratched a name in the dust: “Is mise Sean.” Something is missing — carve it correctly. Type the name as it should be.
blocks.hint: Use the fada keys below the box.

paras: He wipes the dust smooth and says the old spelling law aloud, half chant, half proverb — the rule every Irish writer since has obeyed:
“[Caol le caol agus leathan le leathan.](turas://g/0)”
Slender with slender, broad with broad. From now on, Irish words will look different to you — not like tangles of letters, but like signposted roads.
“Tomorrow,” he says, handing you the chisel to hold — just hold — “we carve.”

glosses.t: Caol le caol agus leathan le leathan.
glosses.g: Slender with slender and broad with broad — the vowels flanking a consonant must agree
glosses.s: kweel leh kweel AH-gus LAH-han leh LAH-han

paras: Dawn, and no wind for once. The pillar lies across two trestles, its edge chalked where the strokes will go. Bríd holds the line taut; Dáire holds the chisel out to you.
“Every stroke you earn,” he says, “you cut.”
Everything you've learned this week is in your hands now.

blocks.prompt: Bríd greets you: “Dia dhuit!” You reply —

opts.why: Raised, not echoed. You've got it.
Raise it: Dia is Muire dhuit.
A lovely phrase — but it's the welcome you give at your own door, not the answer to hello.

blocks.prompt: The widow arrives to watch. Welcome her — build: “A hundred thousand welcomes.”
Dáire quizzes you as you work.
The widow's maiden name was Ní Bhriain. That tells you she was —

opts.txt: a daughter of the Ó Briain family
opts.why: Ní marks a woman of an Ó family — descendant of Brian.

opts.txt: a son of the Ó Briain family
opts.why: Sons carry Ó (or Mac). Ní is the daughter's form.
It's family, not geography — daughter of the descendants of Brian.

blocks.prompt: Bríd chalks the farewell of the dead onto the trestle, but her fadas are missing: “Slan go foill.” Carve it correctly.

paras: By late afternoon it is done. You cut four of the strokes yourself — Dáire guided the chisel but not the choice. The pillar stands; the family stands before it; nobody speaks for a long time.
Along the edge, reading from the bottom up, the way ogham is always read:

blocks.caption: COLMÁN MAC RÓNÁIN — read upward from the base, strokes cut along the stone's edge

blocks.ga: Is buaine focal ná toice an tsaoil.
blocks.en: A word is more enduring than the world's wealth.
blocks.note: Your first seanfhocal — proverb. Dáire's whole trade, in eight words. Collected to your museum.

paras: **Fifteen hundred years later**, a stone very like the one you helped carve is still standing in a field near Killala, County Mayo — the Breastagh ogham stone, leaning into the same salt wind. The farm around it has changed hands a hundred times. The strokes are still legible.
The wealth went. The words stayed. That is the whole story of this app, and you've just lived its first chapter.

**Caibidil a Dó — Oileán na Naomh** is next: a monastery scriptorium at dawn, a race to finish a great gospel book before winter, and a small white cat named Pangur Bán who will teach you the present tense.
You're testing a prototype — after finishing, please tell us: what pulled you back, and what didn't? That answer shapes everything we build next.
